paras: The lynching of Wesley Harrison Smith was the shooting of a Black man near Campbellsburg, Henry County, Kentucky, on the night of Monday, March 7, 1881, by masked "vigilantes" hidden in a barn he was accused of setting on fire. A Cincinnati detective had led him into the trap, and Smith was shot fleeing arrest; he died hours later in a blacksmith shop. The wire version stressed the report that some of the masked men sat on the coroner's jury.

According to a March 8 Campbellsburg dispatch to the Cincinnati Enquirer, at least ten fires had occurred near the town in twelve months, "and not one by accident." About five weeks earlier, the barn and new house of a farmer named Garby had both burned. Neighbors attributed large footprints at the ruins to Smith, a Black neighbor six feet three inches tall, and local businessmen summoned Ben Hatch, a detective of the Ohio & Mississippi Express Company in Cincinnati.

Posing as a buyer for Garby's vacated land, Hatch befriended Smith, whose place adjoined it. In the correspondent's account, Smith said he was "getting even" with Garby and proposed that they burn a barn on Garby's new farm. Hatch agreed and arranged for two leading citizens and an officer to wait in the barn.

On the appointed night Hatch met Smith in a graveyard and went with him to the barn, where, the dispatch said, Smith lit corn stalks and paper soaked in coal oil. Hatch drew a revolver and announced an arrest; Smith ran, and Hatch hit him in the shoulder. At the first shot "a dozen masked men" poured out of the barn, a group that, the correspondent wrote, had gathered without Hatch's knowledge to take Smith "to the first tree" and hang him.

While three or four put out the fire, the rest chased and fired at Smith, and buckshot from one of them brought him down as he climbed a fence. He was hauled in a wagon into Campbellsburg and laid on a cot in a blacksmith shop, where he died at five o'clock.

A coroner's inquest opened on March 8, and the correspondent wrote that some jurors had belonged to the previous night's "Vigilance Committee." He predicted a verdict of "Killed by unknown hands" and no severe punishment. No report of the inquest's verdict or of arrests appears in the coverage.

The Enquirer dispatch ran in the Chicago Daily Tribune on March 10 as "A NEGRO INCENDIARY" and in the Lexington Kentucky Gazette on March 12 as "RECEIVED HIS REWARD. A Barn Burner Shot by Unknown Persons." It treated Smith's guilt as settled, used slurs such as "conceited darky" and "black rascal," and called him "one of Kentucky's worst ruffians."

A shorter Cincinnati telegram, headed "AN INCENDIARY SHOT BY MASKED MEN" in the Washington Evening Star, reported that a "gigantic negro" had been killed by "a band of ten masked men" and that some of the vigilantes were on the coroner's jury. The Alexandria Gazette and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer carried it the same day. Later papers such as the Shenandoah Herald and the Savannah Morning News reprinted it.

The Washington National Republican headed the telegram "Murderers on a Kentucky Jury." The Wilmington Daily Republican instead offered the fires as the explanation: "hence the action of the 'vigilants.'" The Wheeling Register credited the killing to "Detective Ben. Hatch, of Cincinnati, and a number of citizens" and said nothing of masks. A weekly summary in the Gloucester County Democrat, the Narragansett Herald and the Abbeville Press and Banner reduced the story to one sentence about "masked vigilantes" who later "sat on the coroner's jury."
Every version called Smith a "negro" or "colored"; none quoted his family.

Accounts differ on who killed Smith: "a band of ten masked men" in the telegram, Hatch's pistol and then buckshot from one of "a dozen masked men" in the Enquirer dispatch, and the detective and "a number of citizens" in the Wheeling Register. The Enquirer version is the most detailed and was written at Campbellsburg, but it gives the correspondent's and detective's side, recording Smith's words only in his dying remark that he "had been a coon-hunting."

reader.title: Lynching of Wesley Harrison Smith
bases: A Black man accused of barn burning was shot dead at night by a masked band of 'vigilantes' or a 'Vigilance Committee' that had gathered to hang him (A1, A2, A7).

Smith was killed by buckshot from one of a dozen masked, armed men who had gathered without the detective's knowledge to hang him 'to the first tree' for incendiarism (A1, A8); the wire puts the killers at ten masked 'vigilantes' (A2, A7). The killing came during a private detective's attempted arrest with an officer present, and one brief credits the detective and 'a number of citizens' (A6).

All versions appear to descend from the Campbellsburg dispatch of March 8 and a Cincinnati telegram based on it (A1, A2, A7); the Wheeling brief differs on who shot (A6), and no independent local or later report was found.
